_about: PRO rewrite pass 2: era-1 scenes 40-78 in play order.

scenarios.title: The Missed Opportunity
scenarios.text: A bad practice in front of the whole staff: three misses in a row from your favorite spot, the general manager watching from the sideline. By lunch someone in the building is asking about your roster spot.

choices.label: Find out what the staff saw
choices.result: {coach} pulls up the practice film after lunch and freezes it on your plant foot. It's a timing issue, and fixable, and you breathe properly for the first time all day.

choices.label: Kick until the lights come on
choices.result: Long after everyone leaves, you're still out there, kicking until it feels right again. The groundskeeper finally turns the lights on for you and doesn't say a word.

choices.label: Leave it at the facility
choices.result: One practice doesn't define a season, you decide, and you leave it at the facility. Tomorrow is better, mostly, though the general manager's face stays with you on the drive home.

scenarios.title: The Agent Calls
scenarios.text: Your agent calls on a Tuesday night to talk about your contract, your future and a few things you'd rather not hear, starting with the list of reasons rookies get cut before October.

choices.label: Listen to all of it
choices.result: The whole list, start to finish, without interrupting once. It's sobering to hear out loud, and by the end you know exactly which mistakes you're never going to make.

choices.label: Ask for a two-year plan
choices.result: A real plan for the next two years arrives in your inbox by Friday, in writing, with dates. It's the first time your career has looked like something you can steer.

choices.label: Cut the call short
choices.result: Kicking is all you want to think about, so the call ends early. Your agent sends the list by email anyway, and you read it at two in the morning.

scenarios.title: The First Endorsement
scenarios.text: A local car wash offers you your first sponsorship: a billboard by the highway, four appearances in a giant foam sponge costume and a check that's small, but yours.

choices.label: Sign with the car wash
choices.result: The billboard goes up by the highway a week later, a little blurry, and every teammate sends you a photo of it. The holder sets it as his phone background.

choices.label: Ask your agent first
choices.result: Your agent negotiates the appearances down to two and the check up by half. The owner still makes you wear the sponge costume once, and you secretly love it.

choices.label: Keep your weeks clear
choices.result: No billboard, no sponge suit, no appearances. Your weeks stay clear for kicking, your account stays the same, and the car wash signs a local weatherman instead.

scenarios.title: The Old Friend's Request
scenarios.text: {best_friend} calls from home on a Sunday night and asks you for money. It's quiet for a long time before they ask, and you can hear how much it costs them to say it.

choices.label: Send it that night
choices.result: The money is in {best_friend}'s account before you hang up, and you never ask what it's for. They cry on the phone, and so, after the call, do you.

choices.label: Ask what it's for
choices.result: It's rent, three months behind. Paying the landlord directly makes both of you feel better, and {best_friend} sends you a photo of the receipt with a heart on it.

choices.label: Say no kindly
choices.result: No, as kindly as you can manage. It's true and it isn't, and the next phone call with {best_friend} is shorter, and the one after that doesn't come.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Criticism
scenarios.text: {coach} tells you, in front of the specialists, that your preparation isn't professional yet. The punter suddenly studies the floor, and {holder} won't look at you.

choices.label: Ask for specifics
choices.result: Three specific things, you ask for, and {coach} lists them on a whiteboard: film, sleep, and the way you warm up. By November you've done all three, and the coach notices.

choices.label: Show up an hour earlier
choices.result: An hour earlier every day for a month, and you never mention why. {coach} never mentions it either, but your name moves to the top of the practice sheet.

choices.label: Push back
choices.result: Your preparation got you here, you point out. The specialists go very quiet, {holder} gives you a look that says 'not now', and {coach} walks away mid-sentence.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Mistake
scenarios.text: At the team's charity gala, you trip over a cable in front of a dessert table, take the whole thing down with you, and come up wearing a cheesecake. Three cameras catch every second.

choices.label: Laugh at yourself
choices.result: Laughing first saves you. You help clean up, then post the clip yourself with a caption about your leg strength. It's the most popular thing you've ever posted.

choices.label: Pay for the desserts
choices.result: The organizers get an apology and a check for the desserts before the night is over. They're touched, and the event coordinator invites you back to run the dessert table next year.

choices.label: Hope nobody saw
choices.result: Slipping out early doesn't help: the veterans saw, and they leave a slice of cheesecake in your locker every week for the rest of the season. You spend the night at the kicking net.

scenarios.title: The First Charity Event
scenarios.text: The club sends you to a community center's reading day, alone, with a box of picture books and no instructions. Twenty kids sit on a rug, waiting to see what a kicker is for.

choices.label: Read to the kids
choices.result: Sitting on the floor, you read three books in terrible voices, including a very dramatic dragon. The kids demand a fourth, and one of them asks for your autograph on her shoe.

choices.label: Talk about school
choices.result: How hard school was, and why you kept going: you tell them all of it, simply. A teacher finds you afterward and says one boy in the back needed exactly that.

choices.label: Sign and leave on time
choices.result: Autographs, a smile, a group photo, and you're out on time. It's perfectly fine and nobody remembers it, including you, by the following week.

scenarios.title: The Social Media Post
scenarios.text: An old post from college resurfaces the week your name starts showing up in the papers. It's not terrible, but it's not who you are now, and a fan account has just shared it to fifty thousand people.

choices.label: Delete it and apologize
choices.result: Deleted, then a short apology in your own words, no statement from a publicist. It fades in a day, and two teammates text that they respected how you handled it.

choices.label: Leave it up
choices.result: Silence, and the post stays up. It keeps resurfacing every time your name trends, for a month, and the club's media staff starts sighing when you walk past.

choices.label: Get the media staff's help
choices.result: The club's media staff walks you through it in ten minutes, calmly, like they've done it a hundred times. Nobody remembers the post by Friday.

choices.label: Do what worked before
choices.result: This has happened before, so you know the steps: delete, two honest sentences, practice. It's over by lunch, and the media staff asks if you want a job.
choices.lock_text: having handled an old post the right way before

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Party
scenarios.text: A teammate is throwing a party the night before a seven o'clock workout, and the whole rookie class is going. Your phone has been buzzing about it since lunch.

choices.label: Go for an hour
choices.result: An hour of saying hello, then home before ten. Two rookies call you boring in the group chat. In the morning meeting, you're the only one who can keep their eyes open.

choices.label: Sleep instead
choices.result: Nine hours of sleep, and the stories at breakfast are all yours to enjoy secondhand. You feel completely fine about missing them, which surprises you a little.

choices.label: Stay until the end
choices.result: Three in the morning, and you're still there. The workout is a blur, {coach} asks if you're sick, and you tell the truth, which somehow makes it worse.

scenarios.title: The New City
scenarios.text: Two months in {town}, and you've seen the facility, the grocery store and the inside of your apartment. Your blinds have been closed since September.

choices.label: Explore one neighborhood a week
choices.result: A different neighborhood every week, on foot, with no plan. By midseason you know {town} better than some teammates who grew up here, and you have a favorite bakery.

choices.label: Find one place to belong
choices.result: One diner, one gym and one coffee shop, every week, until the people there know your name. It's small, and it's the first time {town} feels like yours.

choices.label: Keep the blinds closed
choices.result: The apartment stays dark between practices. It's restful and easy, and {town} stays a stranger you drive through on the way to work.

scenarios.title: The Family Visit
scenarios.text: {parent} and {sibling} want to visit for a weekend in October. Your schedule doesn't have a weekend in it, and {parent} has already looked up flights and a hotel near the stadium.

choices.label: Make it work
choices.result: The guest room, practice in the morning, every evening with them. You're exhausted by Sunday and happier than you've been in weeks, and {sibling} cries a little at the airport.

choices.label: Ask them to wait for the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, you promise, with a whole week. {parent} understands right away; {sibling} is disappointed and says so, and doesn't text you for a few days.

choices.label: Bring them to practice
choices.result: Two passes to practice and lunch with the team. {sibling} meets the quarterback and talks about it for months, and {parent} keeps the visitor badge on the fridge.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Attention
scenarios.text: Someone recognizes you in the cereal aisle and follows you through three more aisles, talking the whole time about a kick you made in college that you barely remember.

choices.label: Be gracious
choices.result: Stopping costs you ten minutes and a photo by the frozen peas. It makes someone's week, and they post it with a caption about how nice you are.

choices.label: Keep moving, politely
choices.result: A smile, a thank-you and you keep moving. They post that you were 'a little cold', and three people you've never met argue about it for a day.

choices.label: Shop at night
choices.result: Eleven at night becomes your shopping hour. Nobody recognizes you, the cereal aisle is yours alone, and the night cashier starts saving you the good bananas.

scenarios.title: The Local Radio Appearance
scenarios.text: A sports radio show invites you on, live, during drive time. The host is famous for getting rookies to say things, and the producer has warned you there'll be callers.

choices.label: Prepare and go
choices.result: Three stories prepared, all light, and you stick to them. The host can't get anything controversial out of you, laughs anyway and invites you back next month.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.result: No notes. One joke lands beautifully; one answer about the coaching staff gets replayed all week, and {coach} mentions it, dryly, in the next meeting.

choices.label: Spend the hour at the net
choices.result: A polite no, and the hour goes to the kicking net instead. The host makes a joke about shy kickers on air, and you never hear it.

scenarios.title: The Practice Routine
scenarios.text: Your college routine isn't working at this level: too slow for the snapper, too long for the play clock. You need a new one by Sunday, and the veterans are watching to see what you build.

choices.label: Borrow the snapper's rhythm
choices.result: The veteran snapper's pre-kick rhythm becomes yours, step for step. It feels strange for two days, then it feels like it was always yours, and he's quietly proud.

choices.label: Build your own
choices.result: From scratch, charting every kick for a week in a notebook. The new routine is yours entirely, and it holds up when the stadium gets loud.

choices.label: Build it with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} spends an hour with you after practice, building it piece by piece. The coach is clearly pleased you asked, and starts asking your opinion in meetings.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Upgrade
scenarios.text: A sales rep corners you after practice with expensive training equipment: a sensor suit, a kicking machine, and an app that charts every kick you've ever taken. He has a tablet and a very good smile.

choices.label: Buy the full setup
choices.result: All of it, delivered Thursday. The data is incredible, your living room is full of machines, and the bill is the kind you read twice.

choices.label: Use what the club has
choices.result: The club's staff charts you with what they already have. It's less fancy and nearly as good, and the trainer likes being asked.

choices.label: Keep it simple
choices.result: Your leg doesn't need an app, you decide. The rep leaves his card, your weeks stay simple, and you never think about sensor suits again.

scenarios.title: The First Contract Question
scenarios.text: A reporter asks at your locker whether you expect a contract extension. You haven't kicked a regular-season game yet, and the veteran kicker you replaced is standing two lockers away.

choices.label: Joke about keeping your locker
choices.result: Just trying to keep your locker, you say, and grin. The quote is charming, nobody reads into it, and the veteran two lockers down actually laughs.

choices.label: Say you've earned a look
choices.result: You think you've earned a look, you say. The front office reads it by dinner, and so does the veteran, who stops saying good morning.

choices.label: Leave contracts to your agent
choices.result: Contracts are your agent's job. It's dull and smart, the reporter moves on, and {coach} gives you a small nod across the room.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Struggle
scenarios.text: A fellow rookie is falling apart: late to meetings, quiet at lunch, gone the minute practice ends. Yesterday he forgot his helmet. Nobody's said anything to him yet.

choices.label: Knock on his door
choices.result: His door, after practice, and you stay for an hour. He doesn't say much about what's wrong, but he's early to the next meeting, and he sits next to you.

choices.label: Tell a veteran
choices.result: A veteran you trust hears about it quietly, from you. The veteran handles it better than you could have, and the rookie never finds out who spoke up.

choices.label: Mind your own business
choices.result: Your own roster spot is enough to worry about. He's released a month later, and you think about that empty locker longer than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Family Expectations
scenarios.text: Your family expects more now that you're earning. Cousins call about cars, an uncle about a boat, and {parent} about a roof that's been leaking since you were in high school.

choices.label: Set a family budget
choices.result: A yearly amount for family help, set at the kitchen table with {parent}. It's an awkward hour, and it ends the guessing, and the cousins stop calling about cars.

choices.label: Say yes to everything
choices.result: Yes to every request. It feels wonderful for a month, and your account feels it much longer, and nobody says thank you for the third one.

choices.label: Say not yet
choices.result: A rookie contract isn't forever money, you explain, as patiently as you can. Some of them understand. {sibling} doesn't, and says something you'll both remember.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Bill
scenarios.text: Your car's transmission dies the week before a road trip, in the facility parking lot, in front of the whole offensive line. The repair costs more than the car is worth.

choices.label: Fix it
choices.result: Repaired, and a week of buses to practice in the meantime. The veterans think it's hilarious and start leaving bus schedules in your locker.

choices.label: Buy something new
choices.result: A brand-new car the same afternoon. It's lovely, it smells incredible, and the payment is going to follow you around for years.

choices.label: Ride with a teammate
choices.result: Rides with a teammate until you figure it out, and the drives turn into the best part of your week. By the time your car is fixed, you're friends.

scenarios.title: The Former Coach Calls
scenarios.text: Your old college coach calls on a quiet Wednesday night to check in. After the small talk, there's a pause, and then the question: how are you really doing?

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.result: Harder than you expected, you admit. Your old coach tells you about every player who said the same thing in their first year, and made it anyway.

choices.label: Say it's great
choices.result: Everything's great, you insist. Your old coach doesn't believe you, says so kindly, and leaves the door open for another call.

choices.label: Ask for help with one thing
choices.result: One specific problem: your timing on short kicks. Your old coach watches your practice film that night and calls back the next morning with an answer.

scenarios.title: The Community Invitation
scenarios.text: A local high school asks you to speak to its athletes about what it takes to make it. The gym will be full, the principal has put your photo on the marquee, and you've never given a speech.

choices.label: Speak honestly
choices.result: The cuts, the doubts, the practice you nearly quit: all of it comes out, simply. Three kids stay after with questions, and one of them is the school's kicker.

choices.label: Run a clinic instead
choices.result: No speech: a kicking clinic on their muddy field instead. Everyone gets filthy, the principal joins in, and the kids remember it better than any speech.

choices.label: Send your regrets
choices.result: The schedule's too full, you explain. They invite a retired linebacker instead, and you see the photos later and wish you'd gone.

scenarios.title: The Dating Question
scenarios.text: Someone you meet at a teammate's dinner party seems much more interested in the league than in you: salaries, famous teammates, whether you can get them into the owner's box.

choices.label: Ask them out anyway
choices.result: The date happens, and they ask a lot about the league and a little about you. You don't call again, and you learn to recognize it faster next time.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Every time football comes up, you steer away from it. By dessert, they're laughing at your terrible cooking stories, and you realize you're having a good time.

choices.label: Thank the host and go
choices.result: An early thank-you to the host, and you drive home. You'd rather be bored than be someone's résumé, and the drive home is peaceful.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Celebration
scenarios.text: The locker room has a social life: a card game in the back, a weekly dinner, a group that goes out after home games. Everyone's waiting to see how far into it the new kicker wants to go.

choices.label: Join in, within reason
choices.result: The card game and the weekly dinner, yes; the late nights, no. By midseason you're part of the room, and nobody minds that you leave at ten.

choices.label: Pick one thing
choices.result: Just the weekly dinner. You know a few teammates well instead of all of them a little, and two of them become real friends.

choices.label: Keep to your routine
choices.result: Your routine, and nothing else: film, sleep, practice. Your kicking is sharp, and by October nobody in the room thinks to invite you anywhere.

scenarios.title: The Position Meeting
scenarios.text: Your place on the depth chart came up in a meeting you weren't invited to. The long snapper tells you about it at lunch, quietly, then goes back to his sandwich.

choices.label: Ask where you stand
choices.result: {coach} gives you an honest answer in the hallway: safe, for now, if the next month looks like the last one. It's not comfortable, and it's clear.

choices.label: Kick and say nothing
choices.result: Silence, and the best week of practice you've had since camp. Nobody calls another meeting about you, and the snapper starts eating lunch at your table.

choices.label: Call your agent
choices.result: Your agent calls the general manager, who calls {coach}. By Wednesday everyone in the building knows you asked, and {coach} is cooler with you for a while.

scenarios.title: The New Playbook
scenarios.text: A new coaching staff arrives with a new playbook and new expectations for the specialists: three hundred pages, eleven new formations, and a written test on Friday.

choices.label: Learn it cold
choices.result: Every page, cold, including the parts that aren't yours. The new coordinator notices you correcting a linebacker in the walkthrough and remembers your name.

choices.label: Learn your part
choices.result: Your part, perfectly, and nothing else. It's enough for the test, and you get a full night's sleep before it.

choices.label: Study with the unit
choices.result: A study session with the snapper and {holder} turns into a unit dinner, then a weekly tradition. Everyone passes, and you all argue about formations over dessert.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Comparison
scenarios.text: Every week, the local media compare you with another young kicker by name, in charts and columns and one very loud radio segment. You've never met him.

choices.label: Call the other kicker
choices.result: A phone call, and you're both laughing within a minute. You agree not to read anything with both your names in it, and to have dinner when your teams play.

choices.label: Put the charts on your locker
choices.result: The comparison goes up on your locker, and every practice becomes a contest. You're sharper by November, and a little more tired.

choices.label: Stop reading it
choices.result: No columns, no charts, no radio. It takes real discipline for two weeks, then it's just quiet, and you stop wondering how the other kicker is doing.

scenarios.title: The Charity Donation
scenarios.text: Your aunt calls from home: the church you grew up in needs a new roof, and she's sure you'll want to help. She has already told the whole congregation you're thinking about it.

choices.label: Give generously
choices.result: More than she asked. The church puts your name on a brass plaque by the door, which you'll be embarrassed by forever, and {parent} visits it every Sunday.

choices.label: Give what you planned
choices.result: The amount in your budget, with an explanation. She's a little disappointed and grateful anyway, and the roof gets fixed by spring.

choices.label: Run a fundraiser at home
choices.result: A fundraiser in your hometown, run with {sibling}, raises twice the money with your time instead of your account. The whole town shows up.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Advice
scenarios.text: A veteran tells you, very calmly, at lunch, how fast a career can end: his roommate from his rookie year lasted one season and now sells insurance two towns over.

choices.label: Ask what he did differently
choices.result: What did he do differently? His answer has nothing to do with kicking: he saved, he slept, he showed up early, and he never thought he was safe.

choices.label: Let it scare you
choices.result: It scares you, properly. You start saving half of every check and sleeping nine hours a night, and you check the transaction wire more than you should.

choices.label: Shrug it off
choices.result: It won't happen to you, you say with a shrug. The veteran nods slowly, like he's heard exactly that before, and finishes his lunch.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Warning
scenarios.text: Your agent warns you to be careful about where you're seen: a teammate's photo outside a nightclub at two in the morning just cost him a sponsor and a fine.

choices.label: Change your routine
choices.result: No more nights out after home games. You're bored some Saturdays and safe all of them, and the club's media staff stops looking nervous when you walk in.

choices.label: Get the real list
choices.result: A specific list of what's actually off-limits, from your agent, by text. It's shorter than you feared, and much clearer than 'be careful'.

choices.label: Brush off the warning
choices.result: You're not doing anything wrong, you insist, and keep your routine. Your agent sighs and sends a second email with the word 'please' in the subject line.

scenarios.title: The Apartment Neighbor
scenarios.text: Your neighbor works nights and practices drums at noon, which is the only hour of the day you have for a nap. It's been two weeks, and he's getting better, which is worse.

choices.label: Knock and explain
choices.result: A knock, a short explanation, and it turns out he's a fan. He moves practice to the evening and leaves two tickets to his band's show on your mat.

choices.label: Call the building manager
choices.result: The building manager makes the drumming stop within a day. So does the neighbor's friendly wave in the hallway, permanently.

choices.label: Buy good earplugs
choices.result: Very good earplugs, and you nap anyway. It works, mostly, and the neighbor waves at you every morning, never knowing.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Criticism
scenarios.text: Somebody posts a week of your bad practice clips online, set to sad music, and fans tear into you in the replies. {parent} has found it, and has been replying to strangers.

choices.label: Log off
choices.result: The apps are deleted for a week. It's quiet and it helps, and you call {parent} to ask him, gently, to stop arguing with strangers on your behalf.

choices.label: Reply with humor
choices.result: A joke about your own form, in reply, with a slow-motion clip of your worst miss. It's the most-liked reply of the week, and the tone changes.

choices.label: Save the worst one
choices.result: A screenshot of the worst reply goes on your locker. Every rep that week has a little extra in it, and the clips stop coming.

scenarios.title: The Second Contract Conversation
scenarios.text: Your agent starts talking, over a long lunch, about what your second contract could look like if you last that long. There's a napkin with numbers on it.

choices.label: Ask what lasting looks like
choices.result: What does the club actually look for in a second contract? The list is specific, and you can work on every item, starting tomorrow.

choices.label: Dream a little
choices.result: The house, the car, the security: you let yourself picture all of it. It's motivating, mostly, and you keep the napkin.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Not past this season, you say, and push the napkin back. Your agent grins and says that's exactly the right answer.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Rules
scenarios.text: The veterans post the locker room's unwritten rules on a whiteboard, and one of them is about you, in red marker: 'Kickers don't talk in team meetings.'

choices.label: Laugh and follow it
choices.result: Laughing, you follow it all season. The veterans are a little disappointed you didn't fight it; they'd already planned their responses.

choices.label: Break the rule once
choices.result: Once, in a meeting, about something that matters. The room is silent, then a captain nods, and the rule is quietly erased the next morning.

choices.label: Erase it
choices.result: Erased, during lunch. It's back the next morning in bigger letters, with a drawing of you, and the whole team signs it.

scenarios.title: The Playbook Test
scenarios.text: The special teams coordinator quizzes the rookies on the playbook, out loud, at seven in the morning, in front of the veterans. He starts with you.

choices.label: Know it cold
choices.result: Every question, answered cleanly. The coordinator moves on quickly to the next rookie, which is the highest compliment he gives.

choices.label: Bluff through it
choices.result: Two answers bluffed with confidence. The coordinator knows, and assigns you a page of the playbook to copy by hand, in pen, by Monday.

choices.label: Admit you don't know
choices.result: One answer you don't know, and you admit it and ask for the right one. The coordinator respects it, and the veterans notice.

scenarios.title: Learning the Snap Count
scenarios.text: The long snapper's rhythm is completely different from anything you had in college: faster, flatter, with a pause you can't predict. Practice is tomorrow, and the snapper doesn't do small talk.

choices.label: Ask for extra snaps
choices.result: Fifty extra snaps after practice, and he agrees with a grunt. By the end, you can hear the rhythm in your sleep, and he nods once on the way out.

choices.label: Adjust your timing alone
choices.result: Counting in your head all evening, you rebuild your approach alone in the living room. It works by the second day, mostly.

choices.label: Ask the snapper to adjust
choices.result: Can he speed up for you? He laughs and says no. Then, the next morning, without a word, he does it anyway.

scenarios.title: The Wind Tunnel
scenarios.text: The stadium's wind swirls in a way no film can show: in from the left at the bottom, out to the right at the top. The veterans just laugh when you ask about it.

choices.label: Kick in it every day
choices.result: Every day after practice, you kick into the swirl until you can feel it before it moves the ball. Your leg is sore, and the swirl stops surprising you.

choices.label: Ask the grounds crew
choices.result: The grounds crew have watched that wind for twenty years. They show you exactly which flags to watch, and one of them draws you a map on a napkin.

choices.label: Listen at lunch instead
choices.result: Instead of asking, you listen at lunch. Three veterans tell you everything about the wind, one story at a time, over a week.

scenarios.title: The Scout Team
scenarios.text: You spend practice kicking for the scout team, against the starters, and nobody important watches. The coaches are at the other end of the field.

choices.label: Treat it like the real thing
choices.result: Every scout-team rep, like it's the real thing. Nobody watches, and you get better anyway, and the scout-team players start cheering your makes.

choices.label: Get to know the scout team
choices.result: Every name on the scout team, learned by Friday. They become your favorite people in the building, and they save you a seat on the bus.

choices.label: Save your leg
choices.result: Easy reps, and your leg stays fresh. It's sensible, and you notice by Thursday that you don't feel like part of anything.

scenarios.title: The Weight Room Pecking Order
scenarios.text: The weight room has a pecking order, and rookies lift last, after the linemen are done with every rack. By the time you get a bench, it's lunch.

choices.label: Lift at dawn
choices.result: Six in the morning, before the linemen arrive. It's lonely and very effective, and the strength coach starts unlocking the door for you.

choices.label: Spot a lineman
choices.result: An offer to spot a veteran lineman, and he accepts with suspicion. By the end of the week, he's saving you a rack and calling you 'kicker' fondly.

choices.label: Take what's left
choices.result: Whatever's free, without making a thing of it. Nobody notices you, which is fine for now, and you finish your lifts on the stretching mats.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Manager
scenarios.text: The equipment manager can make your life easy or miserable: cleats, balls, the locker by the heater or the one by the door. You've been here a week and haven't said hello.

choices.label: Bring coffee
choices.result: Coffee for the equipment staff on Monday, and you learn every name. Your cleats are perfect all season, and you end up in the locker by the heater.

choices.label: Ask how the balls are prepared
choices.result: How are game balls prepared? He tells you all of it, for an hour, with visible joy. You learn more about kicking than you expected.

choices.label: Keep it professional
choices.result: Hello, thank you and nothing more. It's fine, nothing special happens, and your locker stays the one by the door.
